GOC.title: A 13-year-old gave up his queen and won #shorts
GOC.desc:
On 17 October 1956 in New York, 13-year-old Bobby Fischer had Black against Donald Byrne, one of the best players in America. Byrne attacked his queen, and Fischer left it there and played 17...Be6!! instead. Byrne took the queen, and Fischer's pieces chased the white king across the board until checkmate on move 41. It became known as the Game of the Century. A year later, Fischer won the US Championship at just 14.
Free on iPhone and Android: joker-chess.com

Would you have taken the queen?

It became known as the Game of the Century. A year later, Fischer won the US Championship at just 14.

Top chess rarely looks like this anymore: players prepare their openings with engines, and most games end in a draw. People keep trying to fix this. In Chess960 the back row starts in a random order, so memorized openings stop working (Bobby Fischer introduced it in 1996). Now another variant is gaining popularity: Joker Chess. Each player gets one extra move per game: a queen, rook, bishop or knight can jump to any empty square, without capturing or giving check. It can start an attack out of nowhere. It started with two friends at a wooden board (the last photos are theirs), and they liked it so much that they built an app. It's on the App Store and Google Play.

KRM.title: The world champion missed mate in one #shorts
KRM.desc:
On 27 November 2006 in Bonn, world champion Vladimir Kramnik played game two of his match against the computer Deep Fritz. He was the one pressing for a win, but by then the game was close to a draw. After a few minutes of thought he played 34...Qe3, and Deep Fritz answered 35.Qh7, checkmate. Deep Fritz won the match four games to two.
Free on iPhone and Android: joker-chess.com

Have you ever missed a mate in one?

FSP.title: Fischer didn't even show up for game two #shorts
FSP.desc:
In July 1972 in Reykjavik, Bobby Fischer lost the first game of his World Championship match against the Soviet champion Boris Spassky, then didn't show up for game two and lost it by forfeit. Down 0-2, he would only keep playing in a small back room away from the cameras. Spassky agreed, and Fischer won that game. In game six he opened with 1.c4, a move he had hardly ever played, and after Fischer's win Spassky stood up and applauded. Fischer became the 11th world champion, but in 1975 he gave up the title without playing a single game. Later he said top chess had turned into memorization, and in 1996 he came up with a fix: Chess960.
Free on iPhone and Android: joker-chess.com

Would you have applauded your opponent?
